title: Spot the Phishing Email
instructions: Identify phishing attempts by analyzing the sender, content, and urgency.

questions.question: Your bank asks you to verify your account by clicking a link.
questions.hint: Banks do not ask for information through links.

questions.question: An email from HR asks for your ID card image to update records.
questions.hint: Check if sender's email domain is authentic.

questions.question: You receive a message: 'Your package cannot be delivered. Update info here.'
questions.hint: Delivery scams are common.

questions.question: You receive an email stating: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours. Click here to verify now!'
questions.hint: Urgent threats are classic phishing tactics.

questions.question: An email claims you won a $500 Amazon voucher without participating in any contest.
questions.hint: Unsolicited rewards = scam.

questions.question: Your bank emails from a Gmail address asking you to update your KYC.
questions.hint: Banks never use Gmail or Yahoo addresses.

questions.question: A message says: 'Your package is out for delivery' from an unknown courier service.
questions.hint: Check if the courier name is real.

questions.question: You receive a PayPal receipt for a payment you never made.
questions.hint: Unexpected payment emails are typical phishing triggers.

questions.question: An email asks you to install a 'mandatory security update' via a link.
questions.hint: Software companies don't email install links.

questions.question: An unknown sender says 'Your computer is infected. Click here to fix it.'
questions.hint: Fear-based emails are suspicious.

questions.question: An email says your Instagram password was reset, but you didn't request it.
questions.hint: Account systems do send real alerts for password resets.

questions.question: A message from your college domain asks you to fill in your ID number on the official website.
questions.hint: Official domain + normal request = safe.

questions.question: A delivery service sends a message saying: 'Verify your address to prevent return to sender.'
questions.hint: Watch for links and incorrect domains.

questions.question: An email from 'security@microsoft-secure.net' warns of login attempts. Should you trust it?
questions.hint: Fake domains often add words like 'secure'.

questions.question: Amazon emails you: 'Your purchase has been shipped.' You did order something yesterday.
questions.hint: Matches user action + real sender domain.

questions.question: Your bank emails from 'alerts@bankindia-support.in' asking for verification.
questions.hint: Look closely at domain endings.

questions.question: A message claims: 'Your UPI will be blocked. Update PAN via this link.'
questions.hint: UPI never sends such requests.

questions.question: Netflix says: 'Payment failed. Update your card here.' The link looks suspicious.
questions.hint: Payment failures NEVER come with external links.

questions.question: A message says your IRCTC ticket is canceled and asks you to 'click to claim refund.'
questions.hint: Most refund redirections are scams.

questions.question: Your bank emails you a PDF statement as usual. No links included.
questions.hint: No links = safer pattern.

questions.question: A Google email claims someone accessed your account from a new device. It includes no links.
questions.hint: Google rarely includes links in alerts.

questions.question: A courier company emails you with a realistic tracking ID but incorrect branding.
questions.hint: Fake branding is a red flag.

questions.question: A fake HR email promises double pay if you update your bank details.
questions.hint: HR will never ask bank info via email.

questions.question: Apple emails from 'noreply@apple.com' saying 'Your device signed in.'
questions.hint: Exact official domain.

questions.question: An email uses your real name but urges you to log in urgently to avoid suspension.
questions.hint: Personalization doesn't guarantee authenticity.

questions.question: A WhatsApp 'security team' emails you from a Gmail account.
questions.hint: Companies do NOT use free email providers.

questions.question: An email claims: 'Your GST account is inactive. Verify KYC urgently.'
questions.hint: Government agencies don't send verification emails.

questions.question: A Google Drive file is shared with you by someone you know, but the title looks suspicious.
questions.hint: Drive shares can be abused.

questions.question: Flipkart emails a delivery confirmation for an order you actually placed.
questions.hint: Matches your actual order.

questions.question: A job portal emails you claiming you are shortlisted, but sender domain looks odd.
questions.hint: Fake jobs use strange domains.

questions.question: 'Your Paytm wallet is locked. Update KYC now.' No official Paytm domain.
questions.hint: Paytm uses official verified domains only.

questions.question: 'Claim your IPL free tickets!' from an unknown promotion email.
questions.hint: Too-good-to-be-true offers = scam.

questions.question: A realistic email signature is used but the sender domain differs from the company.
questions.hint: Domain authenticity > signature.

questions.question: An email perfectly imitates your bank's format but links to 'secure-update-bank.com'.
questions.hint: Homoglyph and clone-domain attacks are advanced phishing.

questions.question: A spear-phishing email includes your full name, address, and workplace details.
questions.hint: Attackers can gather personal info easily.

questions.question: You get a PDF invoice that, when opened, asks you to log in to view details.
questions.hint: Malicious PDFs often imitate login prompts.

questions.question: A fake Microsoft email uses 'accounts.micr0soft.com' with a zero instead of an 'o'.
questions.hint: Homoglyph attacks rely on visual similarity.

questions.question: You receive a voicemail email attachment from a legitimate-looking domain, but the .wav file deploys an executable.
questions.hint: Advanced phishing uses disguised attachments.

questions.question: ‘Your electricity bill is overdue. Pay immediately to avoid disconnection.’ The sender domain is not the official provider.
questions.hint: Check if the domain matches the real electricity board.

questions.question: A university email asks you to verify your student account but the link redirects to a non-university website.
questions.hint: Never log in on external websites.

questions.question: An email claims: ‘Your credit card limit is increased. Click to activate.’
questions.hint: Banks rarely provide limit increases without official app notifications.

questions.question: Dropbox says a file was shared with you. The file name is unusual and sender unknown.
questions.hint: File-sharing links are common phishing methods.

questions.question: You get an internship offer with a demand for an upfront security deposit.
questions.hint: Real organizations never ask for payments.

questions.question: A Discord email notifies a login attempt from a new device. Sender matches discord.com.
questions.hint: Official domain = safe.

questions.question: An email threatens: ‘Your AdSense account will be suspended in 12 hours.’
questions.hint: Google never threatens suspension via email.

questions.question: LinkedIn alerts you of a new connection request, matching your activity timeline.
questions.hint: Real notifications align with user actions.

questions.question: A fake Swiggy refund message urges you to claim your ‘overcharged amount’.
questions.hint: Food delivery scams often use refund tricks.

questions.question: Facebook says: ‘Your Page has violated community standards. Appeal now.’ The link ends in ‘facebook-secure.me’.
questions.hint: Fake Facebook domains often end in .me or .xyz.

questions.question: A courier service sends an invoice attachment for customs fees you weren’t expecting.
questions.hint: Unexpected invoices = caution.

questions.question: Spotify sends an email about new login from Chrome. The sender is 'no-reply@spotify.com'.
questions.hint: Correct domain = safe.

questions.question: An IT admin from your company asks you to reset your password via a suspicious link.
questions.hint: Internal IT never uses external links.

questions.question: A job recruitment email asks for your Aadhaar number to 'speed up verification'.
questions.hint: No legitimate recruiter asks for identification over email.

questions.question: A software vendor offers a free license if you fill out a form requiring personal data.
questions.hint: Free license scams often ask personal details.

questions.question: An email claims your Gmail storage is full and you must upgrade via an attached link.
questions.hint: Google never uses links for purchases—only in-app prompts.

questions.question: The email sender matches the official company but the reply-to address is different.
questions.hint: Mismatch of sender and reply-to = phishing.

questions.question: Slack informs you of unread messages and the link is slack.com.
questions.hint: Check domain correctness.

questions.question: Your mobile service provider sends a bill reminder but the email has spelling errors.
questions.hint: Grammar errors are a common clue.

questions.question: 'Your GST refund is ready. Click to claim.' from a government-looking email.
questions.hint: Governments don't email refund claims.

questions.question: An email shows a password you used years ago and tries to blackmail you.
questions.hint: These are classic data-breach scam emails.

questions.question: Someone shares a Google Doc with you regarding a project you’re currently working on.
questions.hint: Context matters—matches real activity.

questions.question: A fake PayPal support email urges you to confirm your credit card for 'security reasons'.
questions.hint: Phishers often pretend to be PayPal.

questions.question: Instagram claims a copyright violation with a suspicious link.
questions.hint: Fake copyright strike emails are common phishing attacks.

questions.question: You receive a 'failed login attempt' message from an unknown platform you never used.
questions.hint: Unknown services = phishing.

questions.question: ‘Your parcel is detained in customs. Pay this amount to release it.’ Sent by an unknown company.
questions.hint: Fake customs payment scams are widespread.

questions.question: Telegram notifies a login attempt. Sender domain is 'telegram.org'.
questions.hint: Official domain = safe.

questions.question: A random contest email says you won an iPhone just by 'being online'.
questions.hint: Scammers use fake contests to lure victims.

questions.question: A fake recruiter asks you to fill out a Google Form with sensitive information.
questions.hint: Recruiters never ask personal data on Google Forms.

questions.question: A fake Ola Driver Support asks you to verify your identity to avoid ride cancellation.
questions.hint: Phishing often imitates popular apps.

questions.question: A phishing email perfectly mimics your company's HR system and includes details of your coworkers.
questions.hint: Highly targeted attacks (spear-phishing) can appear extremely real.

questions.question: An invoice from a trusted vendor includes a duplicate payment request to a new bank account.
questions.hint: Business email compromise (BEC) attacks alter payment details.

questions.question: A seemingly safe Google Doc asks you to log in again to view the content.
questions.hint: Fake login pages often use embedded frames.

questions.question: A malicious Zoom meeting invite includes a link that imitates zoom.us but actually redirects using hidden characters.
questions.hint: URL obfuscation is common in advanced phishing.

questions.question: A vendor email includes a perfectly valid DKIM signature but the provided link leads to a cloned website.
questions.hint: Even validated emails can include malicious links.

questions.question: You receive a PDF from 'IT Support' saying your account will be locked unless you open the report immediately.
questions.hint: Unexpected urgent PDFs are often malware.

questions.question: ‘Congratulations! You have been selected for a free holiday trip.’ The sender address contains random numbers.
questions.hint: Randomized sender names are typical scams.

questions.question: You get a OneDrive file share from someone you don’t know, and the file name looks suspicious.
questions.hint: Unsolicited shared files should be avoided.

questions.question: A Flipkart delivery attempt mail looks real but includes a shortened URL.
questions.hint: Phishing emails often hide malicious URLs.

questions.question: Google sends you an alert from 'security-noreply@google.com' about a login attempt.
questions.hint: Google uses official subdomains.

questions.question: An email pretending to be from IRCTC shows a refund with a clickable link.
questions.hint: Refund emails with links are common attacks.

questions.question: A parcel delivery message claims incomplete address and asks for a ₹50 correction charge.
questions.hint: Fraudsters often use micro-payments.

questions.question: Your bank's monthly e-statement arrives from the exact official email domain.
questions.hint: Check domain carefully.

questions.question: 'Your ATM card will be blocked soon' email comes from a random support address.
questions.hint: Threat-based emails signal phishing.

questions.question: A Microsoft email requests verification but the link leads to a login page with odd formatting.
questions.hint: Look for formatting inconsistency in clones.

questions.question: A message from a payment app confirms an online purchase you actually made today.
questions.hint: Always check if it matches your activity.

questions.question: A message says: ‘Verify your identity for free cryptocurrency airdrop.’
questions.hint: Crypto scams often use giveaways.

questions.question: Your company’s CEO emails directly asking for urgent financial information.
questions.hint: CEO fraud (BEC) is common.

questions.question: A Spotify email confirms a device login from your city and looks identical to past emails.
questions.hint: Consistency helps identify legitimate messages.

questions.question: Fake WhatsApp support asks for your OTP to verify your account.
questions.hint: No service ever asks for your OTP.

questions.question: An email includes your old password and demands payment to avoid 'exposure'.
questions.hint: Common sextortion scam using leaked passwords.

questions.question: A job offer email contains perfect grammar but offers unusually high salary without interview.
questions.hint: Unrealistic offers = scam.

questions.question: A ticket booking site emails promotions you signed up for earlier.
questions.hint: Marketing messages from subscribed services are expected.

questions.question: A message claims: 'Your Aadhaar has been suspended.' The domain is unofficial.
questions.hint: Government never sends suspension emails.

questions.question: GitHub alerts you of a new SSH key added. The email matches their official template.
questions.hint: GitHub security emails are real when from github.com.

questions.question: A cloned SharePoint link leads to a replica login page capturing credentials.
questions.hint: Cloned corporate portals are sophisticated phishing attacks.

questions.question: A highly convincing government tax reminder includes a digitally signed PDF with fraudulent payment link.
questions.hint: Even signed PDFs can be weaponized.

questions.question: Attackers spoof your company’s internal address and request access to confidential files.
questions.hint: Email spoofing can mimic real users perfectly.

questions.question: A threat actor sends a QR code pretending to be a secure login verification page.
questions.hint: QR phishing (quishing) is on the rise.

questions.question: A message includes your full tax ID and a custom link to a fake revenue portal.
questions.hint: Highly targeted identity-based attacks are extremely deceptive.

questions.question: A Zoom invite uses an internationalized domain name with Cyrillic characters that visually mimic zoom.us.
questions.hint: Homoglyph attacks replace characters with lookalikes.

questions.question: A corporate invoice email contains correct logos, correct sender name, but forged routing details.
questions.hint: Invoice fraud is a high-impact phishing method.

questions.question: Your company receives an email pretending to be the CFO, requesting emergency funds transfer.
questions.hint: This is a textbook Business Email Compromise (BEC).

questions.question: An email includes links that appear safe but actually redirect via encoded tracking URLs to malicious sites.
questions.hint: Hover over URLs to check their true destination.

questions.question: You receive a perfectly mimicked Apple invoice PDF, but the support link goes to 'apple-support-billing.com'.
questions.hint: Clone domains are subtle but dangerous.
